column1: # Banking, payments and bank-IT abbreviations, with the institutions a
# reader of Nepali banking material meets. Written for Gloss. Tab-separated:

column3: The central bank of Nepal, established in 1956. It issues currency, sets monetary policy, and licenses and supervises banks and financial institutions.
Nepal's largest state-owned commercial bank, established in 1966.
The first commercial bank of Nepal, established in 1937.
A state-owned commercial bank of Nepal, originally set up in 1968 to finance agriculture.
In Nepal, an institution licensed by Nepal Rastra Bank: class A commercial banks, B development banks, C finance companies and D microfinance institutions.
The company that runs Nepal's national payment systems, including electronic cheque clearing (NCHL-ECC), the interbank payment system (NCHL-IPS) and connectIPS.
Clearing cheques between banks by exchanging their images and data electronically instead of moving the paper.
A system in which each large-value payment between banks is settled individually and immediately, with finality, in central-bank money.
The only stock exchange of Nepal.
The regulator of Nepal's securities market.
An agency that collects borrowers' credit histories from lenders and reports them to lenders assessing a loan.
The Nepali government body that insures bank deposits and guarantees certain loans.
The currency of Nepal.
The process by which a bank verifies a customer's identity and assesses risk before and during the relationship, required by anti-money-laundering rules.
Laws, rules and procedures meant to stop criminals from disguising illegally obtained money as legitimate income.
Measures to detect and block funds intended for terrorist activity; usually paired with AML.
Checks a bank carries out to identify a customer and understand the purpose and risk of the relationship.
A report a bank must file with the financial intelligence unit when a transaction appears linked to crime.
The national agency that receives and analyses reports of suspicious transactions.
A digital form of a country's currency issued by, and a direct liability of, its central bank.
The central software that processes a bank's daily transactions and keeps its accounts, shared by all branches and channels.
A machine that lets customers withdraw cash and do basic banking with a card and PIN, without a teller.
The place — or the terminal — at which a customer pays a merchant, typically by card or QR code.
A secret numeric code that proves a cardholder's or user's identity.
A code valid for a single login or transaction, usually sent by SMS or generated by an app.
The three- or four-digit security code printed on a payment card, used to confirm the card is present.
The global standard for chip-based payment cards and the terminals that read them.
A QR code is a two-dimensional barcode that a phone camera can read; widely used for payments.

column2: Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication
column3: The cooperative, and its secure messaging network, through which banks send international payment instructions.
A standard format that identifies a bank account across national borders.
The 8- or 11-character code that identifies a bank in international payments; also called a SWIFT code.
A bank's written undertaking to pay a seller on behalf of a buyer once specified documents are presented.
A bank's promise to cover a loss if its customer fails to meet an obligation.
A loan on which the borrower has stopped paying interest or principal for a set period, typically 90 days.
A bank's capital expressed as a percentage of its risk-weighted assets; a measure of its ability to absorb losses.
The share of its deposits a bank must hold as reserves with the central bank.
The share of its deposits a bank must hold in liquid assets such as government securities.
A bank's low-cost deposits; a high CASA ratio means cheaper funding.
A fixed monthly payment that repays a loan's principal and interest over its term.
Money placed with a bank for a fixed term at an agreed interest rate.
The yearly cost of a loan, including interest and fees, as a percentage.
Net profit as a percentage of shareholders' equity.
Net profit as a percentage of total assets.
The total value of goods and services produced in a country in a year.
The international organisation that promotes monetary cooperation and lends to countries in balance-of-payments difficulty.
A system that gathers an organisation's data and reports it to managers for decision-making.
A documented plan for keeping essential operations running during and after a disruption.
A contract that defines the level of service a provider must deliver, such as uptime and response time.
Verifying identity with two or more independent factors — something you know, have, or are.
A question answered by choosing one of several listed options.
Video cameras that send their signal to a limited set of monitors or recorders, used for surveillance.
